slides.text: Your washing machine breaks. The shop tells you a new one is cheaper.
slides.footer: Since 31 July 2026, EU law pushes back on that.

slides.text: That reflex, replace instead of repair, has a name and a price. It is the biggest reason e-waste is now the fastest-growing waste stream on Earth.
slides.footer: And repair has been quietly designed out of a lot of the things we own.

slides.caption: Tonnes of electrical and electronic waste thrown out worldwide in 2019. On current patterns that roughly doubles to about 120 million tonnes by 2050.
Only about 17% of the world's discarded electronics is properly collected and recycled. The rest is burned, dumped, or shipped somewhere with weaker rules.
slides.footer: Plus billions of working phones sitting in drawers, never entering any system at all.

slides.text: None of this is one big villain. It is five ordinary things happening at once.
bullets: More devices: most of us now own several at the same time
Shorter lives: kit gets replaced while it still works
Harder repairs: parts, manuals and tools are often out of reach
Software locks: new features stop running on older hardware
Cheap replacement: buying new is usually the path of least effort
slides.footer: Repair is not losing because people do not care. It is losing because it is made awkward.

slides.text: Whatever the brand, a typical smartphone contains around 80% of the stable elements on the periodic table. Once they are bonded together in one device, they are far harder to separate than they were as raw ore.
Behind every new device sits a mine. Demand for minerals like graphite, lithium and cobalt could rise by as much as 500% by 2050.
slides.footer: Badly managed, that mining pollutes groundwater and displaces communities long before anything reaches a shop shelf.

slides.text: So where does Ireland sit in all this? Better than you might think in one way, and worse in another.

slides.caption: Waste produced per person in Ireland every year. That is the sixth highest in the EU.

slides.text: Now the good news. Ireland has built real collection infrastructure through WEEE Ireland, the country's largest e-waste scheme, running for 20 years.
bullets: Over 609,000 tonnes of electrical waste collected and recycled since 2005
More than 250 million old or broken electrical items kept out of landfill
Over 30,000 tonnes of steel, plastic and glass recovered every year

slides.text: But there is a catch in how success gets measured. EU rules ask member states to collect 65% of the average weight of electrical goods sold over the previous three years. Weight is the whole test.
slides.footer: WEEE Ireland's chief executive Leo Donovan has argued this misses the point: a phone that gets repaired or refurbished counts for nothing, even though it is the better outcome.

slides.text: Which brings us to what actually changed this summer.
slides.footer: The EU's Right to Repair Directive applied from 31 July 2026. Ireland's own regulations followed in August.

slides.text: Ireland's version came in as the Common Rules Promoting the Repair of Goods Regulations 2026. It covers a set list of everyday products.
slides.bold: a set list of everyday products

slides.text: The core of it is simple. If a covered product can technically be repaired, the manufacturer now has to repair it when you ask, free or at a reasonable price, and as soon as practicable.
slides.bold: has to repair it when you ask
slides.footer: It also has to publish its repair information. And this applies even after the shop's liability period has run out.

slides.title: What changes when something breaks
bad: Parts priced so high repair made no sense
good: Parts at prices that do not deter repair
No tricks to block a legitimate repair
A written quote that holds for 30 days

slides.text: There is one detail worth knowing about. Second-hand, compatible and even 3D-printed spare parts are allowed, as long as they meet safety standards.
slides.footer: That matters most for older models, where the original maker has stopped producing parts.

slides.caption: Extra months of legal guarantee if you choose repair instead of replacement while the seller is still liable. Choosing the greener option no longer costs you cover.

slides.text: There is also a new piece of paper: the European Repair Information Form. A repairer can hand it to you before you commit to anything.
bullets: It sets out the fault, the fix, the price and the timeline
It is free, unless diagnostics are needed and flagged in advance
Once given, the terms bind the repairer for 30 days

slides.caption: The €4.8 billion in growth and investment the European Commission expects these rules to unlock, because repair is labour that mostly stays local.
slides.footer: Enterprise Minister Peter Burke made the same point about opportunities for Irish repair and refurbishment businesses.

slides.text: And it has teeth. In Ireland the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission enforces the rules and can issue compliance notices. Serious breaches can lead to fines and criminal sanctions.
slides.footer: A pan-European repair platform is expected online in 2027.

slides.text: None of this helps if you cannot find someone to do the work. Ireland already has a free directory for exactly that.
slides.footer: RepairMyStuff.ie is run by Monaghan County Council with the EPA and the Local Authority Waste Prevention Network. It is being built up into Ireland's official national repair platform, due to be fully compliant by 31 July 2027.

slides.text: Search your county, pick your category, from phones and laptops to fridges, furniture, clothes and instruments, and see who near you can fix it.
slides.bold: see who near you can fix it
slides.footer: The law changed the defaults. The next bit is just us using it.
